title: Firewalls with iptables
summary: Chains, default deny, stateful rules, and building a real segmentation policy without locking yourself out.

steps.title: Chains
body: Linux's firewall (netfilter, driven by `iptables`) sorts packets into chains:
Each chain is a list of rules checked **top to bottom**; the first rule that matches decides. If nothing matches, the chain's **policy** decides.

steps.prompt: Which chain does the router see each packet in?
items: An admin SSHing into the router itself
LAN client browsing the DMZ web server
Ping to the router's LAN address
DMZ server replying to a LAN client

steps.title: Default deny and state
body: - **Default allow**: forward everything, block bad things. You'll always forget something.
- **Default deny**: drop everything, allow what's needed. Forgetting something breaks a feature that someone reports, instead of leaving a hole nobody notices.
You only want rules for who may **start** a connection. The `conntrack` module remembers allowed connections, so one rule lets all their replies back:
iptables -L FORWARD -n -v --line-numbers    # rules with packet counters

steps.prompt: Complete the stateful rule that lets replies to allowed connections back through.
steps.explain: Put it first: most packets are replies, so matching them early is also faster.

steps.prompt: A LAN client can't reach the DMZ web server after your change. What's the quickest way to see which rule is hit?
options: Run `iptables -L FORWARD -n -v --line-numbers`, try the connection, and see whose packet counter went up
Flush all rules and start over
steps.explain: Counters are the best firewall debugger: send one test and look.

steps.prompt: You're configuring a **remote** server's INPUT chain over SSH and run `iptables -P INPUT DROP` first. What happens?
options: Your SSH session freezes: you've locked yourself out
Nothing, existing sessions are always allowed
steps.explain: Add the ESTABLISHED and SSH allow rules first, then set the policy. Keep a second session open, or a console, when changing firewalls remotely.

steps.prompt: Order the commands to safely apply a default-deny FORWARD policy.
steps.explain: Flush (which doesn't reset the policy), add allows, then switch the policy to DROP last.

steps.title: Evaluate a chain
prompt: Write `string Decide(List<string> rules, string policy, string src, string dst, string proto, int dport, bool established)`
that evaluates real iptables rule text, first match wins, else `policy`. Support these matches (all present ones must match):
- `-m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED` matches only when `established` is true (ignore the `-m conntrack` words)
starter: string Decide(List<string> rules, string policy, string src, string dst, string proto, int dport, bool established)
solution: if (!int.TryParse(p, out int n) || n < 0 || n > 255) throw new FormatException("bad octet " + p);
string Decide(List<string> rules, string policy, string src, string dst, string proto, int dport, bool established)
template: Dojo.Eq("DMZ reply allowed by state", "ACCEPT", Decide(dojoR, "DROP", "10.16.2.10", "10.16.1.55", "tcp", 51000, true));
Dojo.Eq("DMZ new connection to LAN", "DROP", Decide(dojoR, "DROP", "10.16.2.10", "10.16.1.55", "tcp", 445, false));
hints: Split each rule into tokens and walk them; each flag consumes the next token with `t[++i]`.
AND every match into one `ok`; `-j` just records the target.
